speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Stamp Duties (Amendment) Bill 2018 will give legislative effect to four main categories of changes to the Stamp Duties Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, such transfers are done via physical records, and stamp duty is levied where applicable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the pervasive use of digital technology, there is potential for more of such transactions to be effected electronically, bringing greater convenience to citizens and businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, the Stamp Duties Act does not expressly provide that an “instrument” has to be a physical instrument to be dutiable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Given its legislative history and the fact that some provisions in the Act operate on the basis of an “instrument” being in a physical form, the amendments will update the provisions and provide for how they are to apply to electronic records.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will ensure that our legislation keeps pace with digitalisation and safeguards Singapore’s revenue where transfers are effected without a physical instrument.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have provided a validation clause to address any potential dispute over past payment and collection of stamp duties that have been made in relation to an electronic record.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The existing Act does not restrict the conditions that the Minister may impose when granting remissions, and it is an established practice today that remissions are granted on the basis of certain conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Failure to fulfil these remission conditions would result in recovery of the stamp duty that had been remitted, with interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: When applying for upfront stamp duty remissions, taxpayers today sign an undertaking agreeing that interest is recoverable should they fail to comply with the remission conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such cases mainly involve housing developers, who are granted upfront remission of the Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty for their purchase of land for housing development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The key terms of the remission conditions require the developers to commence, complete and sell the development within a specified timeframe, failing which, the stamp duty earlier remitted will be recovered, together with interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that compensates the Government for the opportunity cost of the duties it would have received, had the remission not been granted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While the current arrangements have worked well so far, we are making this amendment to make clear that the Government can recover interest when a taxpayer fails to comply with any of the remission conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have provided a validation clause, to again address any potential dispute over the past payment and recovery of interest for a failure to comply with remission conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments will align our legislation with changes made to the stamp duty regime in recent years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, a firm is currently not able to enjoy relief from share duty, if its conversion to a Limited Liability Partnership attracts the Additional Conveyance Duty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Given that the policy intent remains not to charge duties under such circumstances, we have amended the legislation to provide relief from share duty under such circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The last category of change pertains to technical amendments arising from the Ministry of Finance’s periodic review to improve tax policy and administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has an E-stamping system, which is an online portal for taxpayers to declare and pay stamp duties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, the Act requires IRAS to seek the Minister’s approval for changes to the administration of the system, such as determining the information to be furnished by taxpayers under the E-stamping system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will amend the relevant provisions of the Act, to give IRAS the flexibility to make these changes without having to seek the Minister’s approval each time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will enhance IRAS’ flexibility and nimbleness to meet its operational needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a time of rising social and healthcare spending, it is important that we secure this revenue base.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we should also always aspire towards providing more options and greater clarity to liable taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am confident that this Bill will help the Government achieve these goals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill provides for the Stamp Duties Act to be applied to electronic records and details specific rules for its application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a significant step towards a regulatory framework built around a digitised economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The digital world moves quickly, and that creates both opportunity and confusion for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what efforts it has made or will make to educate Singaporeans about the legality of these services?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Over the past few years, Singapore has seen the rise of the financial technology (fintech) industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What has gone less noticed is the rise of a property tech (proptech) industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A 2017 media article profiled several Singapore-based proptech firms, each vowing to transform Singapore's real estate sector with new technology.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Several claim to use blockchain, a technology that decentralises control and ownership.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the startups, Averspace, has an app that connects renters and leasers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Its app offers templates for rental contracts that are signed online and stored using blockchain.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two other startups, Reidao and FundPlaces, allow users to own properties using blockchain in conjunction with complex currency changes or Special Purpose Vehicles, though their services have yet to extend to properties located in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, another startup, InvestaCrowd, is planning to launch a crowdfunding model for Singapore property.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (HSBC) report states that 89% of recent homeowners look for properties online.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet consumers may find themselves unclear on the legalities of these models.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2017, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said only that it was "closely watching" the space.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That same year, Reidao's Chief Executive told the media that it had reached out to MAS when he started the business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He claimed that MAS did not, I quote, "make any real comments" to him because it "lacked legislation to instruct the process".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Young digital firms have shown that they can bring excitement to Singaporeans but also headaches for regulators, as we have seen with the likes of Grab.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taking a proactive approach, especially where Singaporeans' nest-eggs are concerned, may be worthwhile.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, clarifications on the legality of blockchain-based property dealers would provide very useful guidance for Singaporeans navigating these digital frontiers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A commentary written by Lee Liat Yang, senior partner of Dentons Rodyk, suggested that while electronic contracts might become the norm in lower-value rental contracts, people may still shy away from them when buying and selling property over safety concerns.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened that the Stamp Duties Act outlines clear penalties against the falsification of records and that the Bill defines terms, such as electronic signatures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this and in many other digital areas, consumers are charting new waters, and there is enough importance in housing that the Government should provide a lighthouse, if not a map, for the people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I am in support of this Bill that keeps our property regulatory framework up to date with developments on the digital frontier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are not exactly specific to the amendments that are being proposed but they are, nevertheless, important issues which I will touch on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, the Government does recognise the rapid pace of technological developments, including in the emerging proptech sector and the use of blockchains for transactions, be it in financial industry or in the property market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In particular, the Electronics Transactions Act (ETA) was first enacted in 1998 to create a legislative framework for electronic transactions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Amongst other things, it provides for the legal recognition and usage of electronic signatures and electronic records, giving predictability and certainty to electronic transactions and facilitating e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The review includes the relevance of the current scope of the ETA and how to improve clarity with respect to emerging technological developments, like the ones Mr Louis Ng talked about, and business models.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will consult and obtain the views of the industry and the public before revisions are made to the ETA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second issue that Mr Louis Ng raised was about the Government's plan to address concerns on security and reliability of using electronic records to execute real estate transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have a Real Estate Industry Transformation Map (ITM) and, under this framework, the various stakeholders from the Government and the private sector have been coming together to discuss how best to streamline and digitalise property transaction processes, and the implementation roadmap to go about doing this work.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The workgroup consists of key Government agencies and industry representatives across the real estate value chain.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Given the typical sizes of property transactions which the Member also alluded to, this would require very careful study in consultation with the industry and regulators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We believe that such a collaboration will help ensure that the interests of property buyers and sellers can be adequately protected, and we can then build confidence in digitalised property transactions.
